paragraphs.text:
4. Nor did the cowardly Trojans leave the mighty son of warlike Hippolochus
without tears, but they themselves too
before the Dardanian gate set the glorious man
upon a pyre; but him Apollo himself,
lifting him very swiftly from the burning fire,
gave to the swift winds to bear near the Lycian land;
and they swiftly bore him away beneath the glens of Telandrus
to a lovely place, and set a rock above him,
unbreakable; and the Nymphs poured forth the sacred water
of an ever-flowing river, which still the tribes of men
call Glaucus the fair-flowing; but these things, perchance,
the immortals wrought as an honour to the king of the Lycians.
And the Argives groaned for high-spirited Achilles
beside the swift-faring ships; and grief wore upon all,
grievous, and mourning, since they sought after him as their own son,
nor was there in the wide host one without tears;
but the Trojans in turn rejoiced unceasingly, beholding
the one band grieving, and the other consumed in the fire;
and one, exulting, spoke such a word:
"Now to all of us, beyond hope, the son of Cronos from Olympus
has granted joy, who longed to see
Achilles fallen in Troy; for I think
that, with him struck down, the glorious tribes of the Trojans will breathe again
out of the deadly blood and the man-slaying battle;
for ever in his heart he devised destruction for the Trojans,
and dreadfully in his hands raged the deadly spear
stained with grievous gore, nor did any of us,
going against him, look any more upon the Dawn;
but now I think the mighty sons of the Achaeans will flee
to their well-prowed ships, now Achilles is slain;
would that the might of Hector were yet alive, that he might destroy them all,
the Argives, together within their own huts.
So spoke one of the Trojans, rejoicing utterly in his heart;
but another, in turn, prudent of mind, spoke a word:
"You think the deadly host of the Danaans within their ships
upon the murky sea will swiftly flee in rout;
but they will not be afraid, longing greatly for battle;
for there are other strong and mighty men,
the son of Tydeus and Ajax and the mighty sons of Atreus;
these I still dread, though Achilles is slain;
would that silver-bowed Apollo would destroy them,
and then a breathing-space from war and from unseemly doom
would come to us in our prayers upon that day."
So he spoke; and the immortals throughout heaven groaned,
all who were helpers to the strong Danaans,
and veiled their heads in boundless clouds
grieving at heart; but on the other side the others rejoiced
praying to grant the Trojans a heart-pleasing end.
And then to the son of Cronos glorious Hera spoke:
"Father Zeus, lord of the bright thunderbolt, why do you aid the Trojans,
forgetting the fair-haired maiden, whom of old
you gave to godlike Peleus as a dear wife
in the glens of Pelion? And you yourself made for her a wedding
divine, and we all on that day feasted,
the immortals, and gave many very beautiful gifts;
but these you have forgotten, and devised a great grief for Hellas."
So she spoke; but tireless Zeus answered her not at all;
for he sat grieving in his heart and pondering much,
because the Argives were destined to sack
the city of Priam, on whom he devised to grant dread destruction
in grievous war and on the heavy-roaring sea;
and so he pondered, what afterward he brought to pass.
And Dawn reached the deep stream of Ocean,
and over the dark earth came boundless gloom,
when mortals breathe a little from their toil;
and the Argives at their ships took their meal, grieving though they were;
for it is not possible to thrust away from the eager belly
the harsh hunger, when it comes upon the breast,
but at once the swift limbs grow heavy, nor is there any remedy,
unless one satisfy the heart-paining belly;
therefore they took their meal, grieving though they were for Achilles;
for dire necessity greatly urged them all.
And when they had eaten, sweet sleep came upon them,
and loosed the pains from their limbs, and roused strength within.
But when the Bears held their heads toward the east,
awaiting the swift light of the sun, and Dawn awoke,
then awoke the host of the strong Argives,
brooding slaughter and dark doom for the Trojans.
And they stirred like the boundless sea of Icaria
or like the deep dry cornland, when there comes
the boundless rush of cloud-gathering Zephyrus;
so the host stirred upon the shores of the Hellespont.
And then the son of Tydeus spoke to the eager men:
"O friends, if in truth we are steadfast in battle,
now let us the more fight against the hateful foe,
lest somehow they take courage, now Achilles is no more;
but come, with our arms and chariots and horses
let us go about the city; toil will grant us glory."
So he spoke among the Danaans; and mighty Ajax answered:
"Son of Tydeus, you say noble things and not idle words,
urging the close-fighting Danaans to do battle
with the war-loving Trojans, who themselves too are eager;
but we must wait by the ships, until from the sea there come
divine Thetis; for her heart greatly devises
to set fair prizes about her son's tomb;
so yesterday she told me, when she went into the depths of the sea,
apart from the other Danaans; and I trust she is near,
hastening; and the Trojans, even though Peleus' son has died,
will not greatly take courage while I yet live
and you and the blameless son of Atreus himself."
So spoke the noble son of Telamon, nor at all did he know
that after the games a daemon was preparing for him an evil doom,
grievous; and the son of Tydeus answered him again:
"O friend, if in truth Thetis comes upon this day
to set fair prizes about her son's tomb,
let us wait by the ships, holding back the others too;
for it is fitting to obey the blessed gods;
and besides, for Achilles, even against the will of the immortals,
let us ourselves devise to give the honour his heart would love."
So spoke the mighty heart of the warlike son of Tydeus.
And then from the sea came the wife of Peleus,
like to the breeze of dawn; and swiftly she reached
the throng of the Argives, where they waited eagerly,
some to contend in the boundless contest,
and some to gladden their minds and hearts with the contenders.
And among them as they gathered Thetis of the dark veil
set the prizes, bearing them, and urged the Achaeans
straightway to contend; and they obeyed the goddess.
And first among them rose up the son of Neleus,
not eager to toil in boxing
nor in much-wearying wrestling; for his
limbs and all his joints grievous old age had subdued;
but in his breast his spirit was yet firm
and his mind, nor did any other of the Achaeans contend
with him, when in the assembly a strife of words arose;
therefore the renowned son of Laertes too, for his words,
yielded to him in the assembly, and he who was most kingly
of all the Argives, great Agamemnon of the good ashen spear.
Therefore in the midst he hymned the kindly Nereid,
how she was preeminent among all the sea-goddesses
for her grace and her beauty; and she, hearing,
was delighted; and he told of the lovely wedding of Peleus,
which for them the immortal blessed ones together fashioned
about the peaks of Pelion, and how they ate the divine
feast at the banquets, when bearing the godly food
in their ambrosial hands the goddess Hours heaped it up
in golden baskets, and Themis, exulting,
stretched out the silver tables in haste,
and Hephaestus burned the undefiled fire, and round about the Nymphs
mingled ambrosia in golden cups,
and the Graces turned to the lovely dance,
and the Muses to song, and all the mountains were delighted
and the rivers and the beasts, and the imperishable upper air was gladdened
and the very beautiful caves of Cheiron and the gods themselves.
And these things the noble son of Neleus to the Argives,
to all their great desire, recounted; and they, hearing,
were delighted; and he sang the imperishable deeds of blameless
Achilles in the midst of the contest; and the great host shouted around
gladly. And taking up from there the glorious man
he greatly honoured him with fitting words,
how he sacked twelve cities of men along his voyage,
and eleven again upon the boundless land, and how he cut down
Telephus, and the might of glorious Eetion
on the plains of Thebe, and how he slew with the spear Cycnus
the son of Poseidon and godlike Polydorus
and wondrous Troilus and blameless Asteropaeus,
and how he reddened to the full the streams of the river
Xanthus, and covered with countless corpses
all its sounding flood, when the life of Lycaon
he took from his limbs near the echoing river,
and how he subdued Hector, and how he slew Penthesileia,
and also the noble son of fair-throned Dawn.
And these things to the Argives, who themselves knew them well,
he sang, and how he was a giant, and how no man
had strength to contend against him face to face, nor in the contests
of warriors, when the young vie with the feet,
nor in horsemanship, nor in the close-standing fight,
and how in beauty he greatly surpassed the Danaans, and how his might
was boundless, whenever the strife of Ares was roused.
And he prayed to the immortals to see such a son too
coming from that sea-washed Scyros.
And the Argives all gave assent to his words,
and silver-footed Thetis herself, and she gave him horses
swift of foot, which before to Achilles of the good ashen spear
Telephus gave as a gift at the mouths of Caicus,
when, as he toiled, his heart sick with an evil wound,
he healed him with the spear, with which he had struck him as he fought,
the very spear, into the thigh, and drove through the mighty point;
and these Nestor son of Neleus to his comrades
gave; and they to the ships led them, greatly honouring
the godlike king. And Thetis set in the midst of the contest
ten oxen about the race; and with each of these
went fair calves running beneath their teats;
which once the bold strength of tireless Peleus' son
had driven from Ida, trusting in his great spear.
And for these two men rose up, longing greatly for victory:
Teucer first, the son of Telamon, and Ajax too,
Ajax, who was preeminent among the arrow-shooting Locrians.
And quickly they girded their loins about with their hands,
with cloths, and below they hid all, as is the rule,
in modesty before the wife of mighty Peleus
and the other sea-dwelling Nereids, as many as with her
had come to behold the strong contests of the Argives.
And to them the son of Atreus marked the goal of the swiftest race,
who ruled over all the Argives.
And lovely Strife urged them on; and from the starting-line
swiftly they sped, like hawks;
and their race was hard to judge; and on either side
the Argives, watching, shouted, one this way, one that.
But when, eager, they were about to reach the goal,
then indeed the might and limbs of Teucer were fettered
by the immortals; for a god struck him, or some blindness,
on a grievous root of a deep-rooted tamarisk;
and stumbling on it he fell to the ground; and grievously
the end of his left foot was bent back, and there rose up
swollen on either side the veins about it. And they shouted,
the Argives in the contest; and Ajax ran past him
rejoicing; and the peoples ran together, who followed him,
the Locrians; and at once joy came upon the hearts of all;
and they drove the leader's oxen down to the ships, to be tended.
And Teucer his comrades, busily attending him,
led him limping; and swiftly the healers
took the blood from his foot, and laid above on lint
wool well soaked in unguents, and round about
they bound a band carefully; and they scattered his grievous pains.
And again, on the other side, of overweening wrestling
swiftly two strong-hearted men bethought themselves,
the son of horse-taming Tydeus and overbearing Ajax,
who went into the midst; and amazement held the Argives
who beheld them; for both were like to the blessed ones.
And they closed like wild beasts, which in the mountains
fight over a deer, longing for food,
and equal is the might of both, nor does either of them
fall short even a little, harsh though they are;
so they held an equal strong fury. And at last Ajax
seized the son of Tydeus with his sturdy hands,
eager to break him. But he, with skill and might,
bending his side, the mighty son of Telamon
swiftly lifted, pressing beneath the muscle
his shoulder, and tripping his thigh with his foot to the other side
flung the mighty man to the ground; and round about him
he sat; and the people shouted. But vexed in his heart
strong-hearted Ajax rose up a second time again
rushing to the pitiless strife; and swiftly with his hands
terrible he poured dust upon himself, and raging greatly
he called the son of Tydeus into the midst; but he, in no way
afraid, sprang against him; and much
dust rose beneath the feet of both; and on either side
they rushed together like fearless bulls, which in the mountains,
testing their bold might, come to one place
contending with their feet in the dust, and the hills roar around
beneath the bellowing of both, and they, raging unrestrained,
dash together their tireless heads and great might
long toiling against one another, and out of their effort
panting fiercely they contend pitilessly,
and much foam pours down to the ground from their mouths;
so these two toiled to the full with their sturdy hands.
And the backs and strong necks of both
rang beneath their hands, creaking, as in the mountains
trees cast upon one another their flourishing boughs.
And often beneath the sturdy thighs of great Ajax
the son of Tydeus thrust his strong hands, but in no way
could he thrust him back, planted on his sturdy feet;
but Ajax, rushing from above to the ground,
shook him from his shoulders, pressing him down to the floor of earth;
and now this way, now that, they strove beneath their hands.
And the peoples here and there shouted greatly as they watched,
some heartening the glorious son of Tydeus,
others the might of Ajax; and he, shaking the valiant man
from his shoulders on either side, and casting his hands beneath his belly,
swiftly hurled him to the ground like a stone
by his mighty strength; and the Trojan earth greatly resounded
as the son of Tydeus fell; and the people shouted aloud.
But even so he sprang up, longing to toil
a third time about giant Ajax; but Nestor
stood in the midst and addressed them both:
"Cease, glorious children, from overweening wrestling;
for we all know how far you are superior
to the Argives, now great Achilles is slain."
So he spoke; and they ceased from their toil; and from their brows
with their hands they wiped to the full the streaming sweat;
and they kissed each other, and in friendship laid aside their strife.
And to them then lady among goddesses, divine Thetis,
gave four captive women; and the heroes themselves marvelled
to behold them, strong and fearless, since of all
the captive women they were preeminent in grace and in works,
next to fair-tressed Briseis, whom once Achilles
took as spoil from Lesbos, and in his heart delighted in them;
and one of them was steward of the supper and the food,
and another poured for the feasters the sweet wine,
and another again after the supper poured water on their hands,
and the other ever bore the tables from the feast.
And these the might of the son of Tydeus and overbearing Ajax,
dividing, sent to their well-prowed ships.
And about boxing first the strength of Idomeneus
rose up, since his heart was skilled in every contest.
And none came against him; for all,
in respect, yielded to him, since he was the elder.
And to him in the midst Thetis gave a chariot and horses
swift of foot, which before the might of great Patroclus
had driven from the Trojans, slaying noble Sarpedon;
and these Idomeneus gave to his attendant to lead to the ships,
while he himself remained in the glorious contest.
And Phoenix spoke among the strong Argives:
"Now indeed to Idomeneus the gods have given a noble prize
freely, not toiling with might and hands and shoulders,
but honouring without bloodshed the elder man;
but, young men, prepare another contest,
guiding your skilful hands against one another
in boxing, and gladden the spirit of Peleus' son."
So he spoke; and they, hearing, looked at one another;
but quietly all held back, declining the contest,
had not the son of noble Neleus rebuked them:
"O friends, it is not seemly for men skilled in the war-cry
to shun lovely boxing, which to the young
is a delight, and after toil brings glory.
Would that in my limbs there yet lay such strength
as when we buried godlike Pelias,
I myself and Acastus, cousins coming together,
when I was matched against noble Polydeuces
in boxing, and took a prize equal to his;
and in wrestling even the strongest of the others,
Ancaeus, marvelled at me and trembled, nor did he dare
to come against me for victory, because him
already before, among the close-fighting Epeians,
I had conquered, good though he was, and he fell and rolled his back in the dust
beside the tomb of dead Amarynceus; and about him
many marvelled at my might and strength;
so against me no more did he raise his hands,
strong though he was, and I took the prize unsweating;
but now old age comes upon me and griefs; therefore I bid
you, to whom it is fitting, win the prizes with your hands;
for it is glory for a young man to bear a prize from the contest."
As the old man spoke thus, a bold man rose up,
the son of high-souled and godlike Panopeus,
who too made the horse, an evil to the city of Priam,
afterward; but no one dared to come near him
for boxing; yet he was not at all skilled
in grievous war, when the strife of Ares was roused.
And without sweating the noble Epeius would then
have borne the very beautiful prizes to the ships of the Achaeans,
had not there come near him the son of noble Theseus,
the spearman Acamas, raising great might in his breast,
holding dry thongs about his swift hands,
which skilfully Agelaus son of Euenor
had bound about his palms, urging on his king.
And so too the comrades of the lord, son of Panopeus,
heartened Epeius; and he in the midst, like a lion,
stood, holding about his hands the dry hides
of an ox slain by force. And greatly here and there
the peoples shouted, urging on the might of the strong men
to mingle their tireless hands in blood; and they themselves
stood eager at the meeting-place of the contest,
both testing their hands, whether they were
as nimble as before, and not weighed down from the war.
And swiftly they raised their hands against one another,
glancing keenly, and on the very tips of their feet
stepping, ever shifting knee from knee
of one another, long avoiding the great might.
And they closed like swift clouds,
which by the rushes of the winds, leaping upon one another,
send forth lightning, and the great upper air is stirred
as the clouds are sharpened, and the gusts crash heavily;
so their jaws rang round about with the dry
hides; and much blood ran down, and from their brows
the bloody sweat reddened their blooming cheeks.
And they toiled ceaselessly in their eagerness; nor did Epeius
cease, but ever rushed on, raging greatly in his might.
But the son of Theseus, prudent in the contest,
made him often aim his strong hands at the empty air,
and with skill, cutting through on either side,
struck his hands at the brow, leaping in, until he reached
the bone; and from his eye the blood ran down.
But even so Epeius, striking Acamas with his heavy hand,
smote him on the temple, and dashed his limbs to the ground;
yet he swiftly sprang up and leapt upon the mighty man,
and struck his head; but he, as the other rushed at him,
bending a little aside, struck his brow with his left hand,
and with the other dashed his nose, leaping in; and he himself
with every device stretched out his hands; but the Achaeans
held them back from one another, eager though they were to toil
for lovely victory. And their attendants swiftly
loosed the bloody hides from their strong hands
at once; and they breathed a little from their toil,
wiping their brows with many-holed sponges.
And their comrades and friends, comforting them, led them
face to face with one another, that of their grievous wrath
they might swiftly forget, reconciled in friendship.
And they obeyed the soothing words of their comrades;
for to prudent men the mind is ever gentle;
and they kissed each other, and their hearts forgot
the grievous strife. And to them swiftly Thetis of the dark veil
gave, at their desire, two silver mixing-bowls,
which Eunous, the mighty son of Jason,
gave as a ransom for strong Lycaon
to godlike Achilles in sea-washed Lemnos;
which Hephaestus made for glorious Dionysus
as a gift, when he led up to Olympus his divine wife,
the glorious daughter of Minos, whom once Theseus
left, unwilling, in sea-washed Dia.
And these noble Dionysus gave as a gift to his son,
filling them with nectar; and he gave them to Hypsipyle
with many possessions, Thoas, and she to her noble son
left them, and he gave them to Achilles for Lycaon's sake.
And of these the one the son of noble Theseus took,
and the other noble Epeius sent to his own ships,
rejoicing. And all their bruised wounds
Podaleirius healed carefully, since he himself
first sucked them, and then with his own hands
stitched them skilfully, and laid above the drugs,
those which before his father had given him;
and by these swiftly even the unhealing wounds of men
on that same day are eased of their deadly evil;
and at once about their faces and fair-haired heads
the wounds were healed, and their pains were soothed.
And about archery Teucer and the son of Oileus
stood, who before had made trial of the race.
And for these the good-speared Agamemnon set afar
a horse-plumed helmet, and said: "Far the better
shall he be, who shears off the hair with the sharp bronze."
And Ajax at once first sent forth his shaft,
and struck the helmet, and the bronze rang out
very sharply. And Teucer, greatly hastening in his heart,
second let fly his arrow, and at once sheared off the plumes,
the sharp shaft; and the peoples shouted greatly as they watched,
and honoured him boundlessly, since indeed
the blow still pained his swift foot, yet in no way
did it harm beneath his hands as he aimed the swift shaft.
And to him fair arms the wife of Peleus gave,
the arms of godlike Troilus, whom of youths far the best
in holy Troy Hecabe bore, but she had no profit
of his splendour; for the spear of grim Achilles
and his strength together robbed him of life;
as when, in a dewy and flourishing garden,
beside a watered ditch, very near, blossoming richly,
an ear of corn or a poppy, before it reach its fruit,
one shears with a newly-sharpened sickle, nor lets it
come to its sweet end nor reach another sowing,
reaping it empty and seedless for the time to come,
when it was about to grow beneath the dewy spring;
so the son of Priam, like to the gods in form,
Peleus' son slew, still beardless, still of a maiden
untouched, still playing like the little children;
but Fate led him to man-destroying war
at the beginning of joyous youth, when men
grow bold, when the heart no longer lacks.
And straightway again a discus, very long and strong,
many tried to hurl from a swift hand;
but none of the Argives could throw it, being very heavy;
and steadfast Ajax alone threw it
from his strong hand, as the bough of an oak in the field,
withered in the season of warm summer,
when all the cornlands wither upon the ground.
And all marvelled how far from his hand the bronze
flew, which two men toiling had lifted with their hands;
which the might of Antaeus had hurled of old
easily from his hand, testing his strength,
before he was subdued by the strong hands of Heracles;
and noble Heracles, taking it with much spoil,
kept it as a prize of his tireless hand, but to the noble
descendant of Aeacus afterward he gave it as a gift, when with him
he sacked the glorious city of well-towered Ilios;
and he gave it to his son, and he in his swift ships
bore it to Troy, that mindful of his own father
he might fight against the strong Trojans
eagerly, and have toil as he tested his strength;
and this Ajax threw very far from his sturdy hand.
And then to him the Nereid gave the renowned armour
of godlike Memnon, which too the Argives greatly
marvelled at; for they were all exceedingly huge;
and rejoicing the glorious man received them;
for to him alone, about his sturdy limbs,
they fitted, set about his vast flesh;
and he himself in turn lifted the great discus, that it might be
a delight to his noble might, longing to toil.
And contending in the leap many rose up;
and over them all leapt by far the good-speared Agapenor
beyond the marks; and the people shouted at the man who leapt so far;
and to him fair arms of great Cycnus
divine Thetis gave; for him, over the slaughter of Protesilaus,
when he had taken the lives of many, Peleus' son slew,
the first of the chiefs; and grief enwrapped the Trojans.
And with the javelin Euryalus far surpassed
the contenders; and the peoples shouted greatly; for they thought
that none could surpass him even with a winged shaft.
Therefore to him a deep cup to bear away
the mother of warlike Achilles gave, which once Achilles
won as silver spoil, striking down Mynes with his spear,
when he sacked the prosperous city of Lyrnessus.
And strong-hearted Ajax, longing to toil
alike with hands and feet, rising up called
into the midst of the heroes the highest. And they, beholding,
marvelled at the mighty and valiant man; nor did any dare
to come against him; for of all grievous fear had broken
their manhood, and they feared in their hearts, lest, striking some man
with his tireless hands, beneath his blows the face
he should shatter swiftly, and great woe come upon the man.
And at last all gave the nod to steadfast Euryalus,
knowing him well skilled in boxing; and he in the midst
sent forth such a word, trembling before the bold man:
"O friends, any other of the Achaeans whom you wish
I will dare to face, but at great Ajax I am amazed;
for far he excels; he will shatter my heart,
if wrath seize him, rushing on; for I do not think
to come safe to the ships from that tireless man."
So he spoke; and they laughed; and in his heart utterly gladdened
was strong-hearted Ajax; and he raised two talents
of gleaming silver, which Thetis for the contest
gave him without toil; and he remembered his dear son,
beholding Ajax; and lament fell upon his heart.
And they in turn, having their hearts set on horsemanship,
swiftly rose up as the contest summoned them:
first Menelaus and Eurypylus bold in battle
and Eumelus and Thoas and godlike Polypoetes.
And they cast the yoke-straps about the horses and dragged them beneath the chariots,
all hastening for the sake of joyous victory;
and swiftly they came together into one, standing in their cars,
in the sandy place; and each stood at the starting-line;
and quickly they took the reins in their strong hands.
And the horses, drawing close in the chariots, fretted
that one might leap forward, and they stirred their feet thus,
and pricked up their ears, and wet their brow-bands with foam.
And they at once, hastening, lashed the might
of the light-footed horses; and they, like swift Harpies,
swiftly leapt greatly forward from the yokes, chafing,
and the chariots swiftly bore them, darting from the ground;
nor was it possible to see the chariot-tracks nor of the feet
the marks on the ground, so far did the horses carry the race forward.
And much dust reached the upper air from the plain,
like smoke or mist, which in the mountains
the might of the south wind or of Zephyrus pours about the headlands
when a storm rises, when the mountains are wet with rain.
And the horses of Eumelus leapt greatly forward, and there followed
those of godlike Thoas; and one upon another shouted
about his chariot; and they were borne through the spacious plain
. . .
out of bright Elis, since indeed he did a great deed,
outstripping the swift chariot of evil-minded Oenomaus,
who then wrought pitiless destruction for the youths
about the marriage of his prudent daughter Hippodameia;
but not even he, skilled though he was in horsemanship,
had such swift-footed horses, but far
weaker of foot; for these seemed like the winds.
And he greatly glorified the might of the horses and himself,
the son of Atreus; for in his heart he rejoiced in spirit.
And them, greatly panting, the attendants at once loosed
from the yoke; and the others too loosed their wind-footed horses,
all for whom in the contest a strife of the race arose.
And godlike Thoas and Eurypylus bold in battle
Podaleirius swiftly healed of all their wounds,
all that they had scraped, falling from their cars.
And the son of Atreus rejoiced unceasingly for his victory;
and to him fair-tressed Thetis gave a fair goblet
of gold, the great possession of godlike Eetion,
before Achilles sacked the glorious city of Thebe.
And others on the other side were yoking single-frontlet horses,
guiding them to the race, and took in their hands the ox-hide
whips, and all, leaping up upon their horses,
sat; and they champed the bits, foaming at their jaws,
and with their feet stamped the ground, hastening
to dart away. And for them swiftly the race was stretched; and from the starting-line
swiftly they sped, eager to contend,
like the gusts of greatly-blowing Boreas
or of roaring Notus, when it stirs the wide sea
with storm and squalls, when the grievous Altar-star
rises for sailors, bringing much-wept misery;
so they sped, stirring the dust with their swift feet
in the plain, raising it boundless; and the drivers
each called to his own horses, and with the lash
struck thickly with the one hand, and with the other shook
unceasingly the bit clashing greatly about their jaws.
And the horses rushed on; and a shout rose among the host
boundless; and they flew through the broad plain.
And now indeed swiftly from Argos the dappled horse
would have won by far, with Sthenelus mounted on him,
had he not swerved from the course, and reached the plain
many times; nor could the noble son of Capaneus
turn him with his hands, since he was still untaught in contests,
that horse; in breed indeed not base, but of the swift
divine stock of Arion, whom there bore among horses
a Harpy to loud-sounding Zephyrus, far the best of all
by much, since with his swift feet he vied
with the swift gusts of his own father, and Adrastus
had him as a gift from the blessed, whence was that horse's stock;
and the son of Tydeus gave him as a gift to his comrade
in holy Troy; and he, greatly trusting in his feet,
swift though he was, brought him to the contest and to the strife of horses,
himself thinking among the first to win great glory
of horsemanship; but he gladdened not his heart at all,
toiling about the prizes of Achilles; for indeed he stayed
second, and the son of Atreus drove past him, swift though he was,
by his skill. And the peoples honoured Agamemnon,
and the horse of bold-hearted Sthenelus and himself,
because he came second, even though very often from the course
he leapt aside, raging in great strength with his feet.
And then to the son of Atreus Thetis gave, as he exulted,
the silver corselet of god-born Polydorus;
and she gave to Sthenelus the strong helmet of Asteropaeus,
of bronze, and two spears and a tireless girdle.
And to the other horsemen, all who upon that day
had come to contend at the tomb of Achilles,
she gave gifts to all. But over them his heart grieved,
the son of warlike Laertes, because
him, eager for valour, the grievous wound kept back
from the strong contests, which mighty Alcon had dealt him
as he toiled about the corpse of the strong son of Aeacus.

14. And then from Ocean the golden-throned goddess Dawn
sprang up to the sky; and Chaos received the night.
And the Argives by force laid waste well-fenced Troy
and plundered her boundless wealth,
like torrent rivers, which are borne
from the mountains with a roar when the rain is stirred up,
and many tall trees and all that grows in the hills,
with the very headlands, they bear into the sea;
so the Danaans, having sacked beneath fire the Trojan city,
bore all the goods to their swift-bounding ships.
And together they drove off the women of Troy from this side and that,
some still unwed and inexperienced of marriage,
and one new-subdued to love beneath the warriors,
others again grey-haired, and others younger than these,
whose children they had torn from their breasts,
still craving with their lips the last of the milk.
Among these Menelaus himself, in their midst,
led his own wife from the burning city,
having accomplished a great deed; and joy and shame held him.
And good-ashen-speared Agamemnon led off noble Cassandra;
and Andromache the noble son of Achilles; but Odysseus
dragged Hecuba by force; and from her eyes thronging tears,
like a spring, poured down; and her limbs trembled,
and her heart was distraught with fear, and she had torn her hair
from her grey head; and much ash lay upon her,
which she had heaped abundantly with her hands from the hearth
as Priam perished and the city blazed;
and she groaned greatly, when the day of slavery enwrapped her,
dragged off against her will; and one led one wailing woman,
another another, of the Trojan women, by force to their ships;
and they, wailing piteously, cried aloud, one here, one there,
lamenting most grievously together with their infant children;
as when, together with white-tusked swine, men drive the young
from the former steading to another steading
in the rising of a storm, and they, grievously
mingled together, squeal continually to one another;
so the women of Troy, subdued, groaned beneath the Danaans;
and queen and handmaid alike bore equal necessity.
But Helen no wailing enwrapped; rather shame
sat upon her dark eyes, and above
her fair cheeks blushed red; and within her the heart
beat unspeakably in her breast, lest, as she went
to the dark ships, the Achaeans should maltreat her;
therefore, trembling, she quivered in her dear heart.
And, covering her head above with a veil,
she followed in the footstep of her husband as he went,
blushing in her cheek for shame, like Cypris,
when the heavenly ones, in the embrace of Ares,
plainly perceived her dishonouring her own bed
in the close-set bonds of skilful Hephaestus,
in which she lay, grieving in heart and ashamed
before the throng of the blessed ones gathered there, and before
Hephaestus himself; for it is terrible, in the eyes of one's husband,
to be plainly beheld in shame, for womankind.
Like her in form and in undefiled shame
went Helen with the captive Trojan women, she too,
to the well-oared ships of the Argives; and around her the host
marvelled, beholding the splendour and the lovely
beauty of the blameless woman; nor did any dare
to provoke her, neither secretly with abusive words,
nor yet openly, but they looked upon her as a goddess,
gladly; for to all in their longing she appeared.
And as, to men wandering over the unwearied sea,
their own fatherland appears at last to their longing,
and they, having escaped both the sea and death,
stretch out their hands to their country, rejoicing boundlessly in heart;
so all the Danaans around rejoiced; for no longer in them
was there memory of grievous toil nor of turmoil;
for such a mind Cytherea made in them all,
bringing grace to bright-eyed Helen and to Zeus the father.
And then, when he saw his dear city laid waste,
Xanthus, still breathing the bloody din,
mourned together with the Nymphs, since evil had fallen on Troy
from somewhere, and laid low the city of Priam;
as when the dry cornfield, with hail bearing down,
is cut short, and all the ears are stripped away
by the grievous blast, and the stalk is poured on the ground,
the fruit lost in vain upon the soil,
grievously, and great grief comes to the wretched lord;
so also to the heart of Xanthus came grief
as Ilium was left desolate; and misery held him ever,
immortal though he was; and tall Ida groaned around,
and Simoeis; and far off all the haunts
of Ida mourned, wailing for the city of Priam.
And the Argives went to their ships, greatly exulting,
hymning the mighty valour of their glorious victory,
and now the holy race of the blessed ones, and now their own
daring spirit and the imperishable work of Epeius.
And song reached the sky through the air, like the cry
of jackdaws, boundless, when a fair day comes
out of the deadly winter, and the air is calm;
so the heart of those by the ships rejoiced greatly within . . .
and the immortals throughout the sky took delight, all who were helpers
in their hearts of the war-loving Argives;
but others were vexed, all who defended the Trojans,
beholding the city of Priam ablaze;
but they, though longing to help, could not avail
beyond Fate; for not even the son of Cronos himself,
beyond doom, could easily thrust Fate aside, he who of all
the immortals has the most might, and from Zeus all things come.
And the Argives, setting on the altars many thigh-pieces of oxen,
burned them together with the cleft wood, and hastening about the altars
poured sweet wine over the blazing offerings,
bringing grace to the gods, since they had accomplished a great deed.
And much at the heart-cheering banquet they glorified
all who had been received with their arms in the wooden horse;
and they marvelled at glorious Sinon, because he had endured
the much-grievous outrage of the foe; and all of them
honoured him with song and with boundless gifts;
and he in his heart rejoiced, with steadfast spirit,
at the victory of the Argives, and grieved not at his own outrage;
for to a prudent and thoughtful man far better
is glory than gold or beauty or any other
of the good things that are or shall be for men.
And they beside the ships, with fearless hearts,
supped, telling each other continually:
"We have accomplished the end of the long war; we have won broad
glory, having taken with the foe their great city;
but, O Zeus, grant us also the return in our longing."
So they spoke; but the father did not grant return to all.
And among them one, skilled . . .
. . . for no longer in them
was there dread of the ill-sounding war, but to the works
of good order they turned, and to lovely good cheer.
And he indeed first, to their longing, sang
how the host had gathered to the holy ground of Aulis,
and how the great might of unwearied Peleus' son
went over the sea and sacked twelve cities,
and eleven again over the boundless land, all that he wrought
about lord Telephus and mighty Eetion,
and how he slew overweening Cycnus, and all that the Achaeans
in the wrath of Achilles wrought as they fought,
and how he dragged Hector about the walls of his own fatherland,
and how he took Penthesileia in the fray, and how he subdued
the son of Tithonus, and how strong Ajax slew
good-ashen-speared Glaucus, and how the glorious man
Eurypylus the son of swift Aeacides slew,
and how the shafts of Philoctetes laid low Paris,
and all the men who went within the guileful horse,
and how, having sacked the city of god-born Priam,
they feasted, far apart from evil turmoils.
And this man sang one thing, that man another, whatever was in his heart.
But when, as they feasted, the middle of night came round,
then indeed from supper and from the strong drink
all ceased, and took care-banishing sleep;
for the strength of yesterday's toil overcame them all;
and so, though they had longed to feast all night long,
they ceased, since sleep against their will held them fast;
and one slept here, another there; but in his own hut
the son of Atreus conversed with his fair-haired wife;
for not yet had sleep fallen upon their eyes,
but Cypris was busy about their hearts, that they might remember
their old marriage-bed, and cast their grief away.
And first Helen spoke a word like this:
"Do not now, O Menelaus, set wrath against me in your heart;
for it was not of my own will that I left your home and bed,
but the might of Alexander and the sons of Troy
snatched me away, coming while you were far off,
and, though I was utterly eager to perish wretchedly
either by a grievous noose or by a groaning sword,
they kept me in the halls, comforting me with words,
grieving for you and for my well-loved daughter;
by her, then, and by our marriage of much joy and by yourself
I beseech you, to forget your hateful anger against me."
To her as she spoke wise Menelaus answered:
"No longer now remember it, but hold your griefs in your heart;
but let the black house of forgetfulness shut all these things
within; for it is not fitting to remember evil deeds any longer."
So he spoke; and joy seized her, and fear rushed from her heart;
for she hoped that her husband would cease from grievous wrath;
and she cast her arms about him; and from them both alike
sweet tears flowed down their eyelids as they wept.
And gladly the two of them, reclining beside one another,
remembered in their hearts their own marriage;
as when ivy and the cultivated vine cast themselves
about one another round the trunks, and never can the force of the wind
hurl them apart; so the two of them
held to one another, longing for love.
But when sleep, free from harm, came upon them too,
then the strong heart of godlike Achilles
stood over the head of his son, just as he was
when alive, when he was a grief to the Trojans, a joy to the Achaeans.
And he kissed his neck and his gleaming eyes
gladly, and, comforting him, spoke:
"Hail, my child, and do not rend your heart with grief
because of my death, since with the blessed gods
I am now a fellow at the hearth; but restrain your heart, sore-tried
for me, and set my strength to the full in your spirit.
Ever stand as foremost of the Argives, yielding to none
in manhood; but in the assembly to the elder men
give heed; and then all will call you wise.
Honour the blameless men, all whose mind is steadfast;
for to the noble a noble man is dear, and to the harsh, grievous.
If you think good thoughts, you will achieve good deeds too;
for that man never reached the goals of Virtue
who has not a righteous mind; because her
trunk is hard to climb, and far up to the clear sky
her branches grow; but those whom strength attends
and toil, from labour reap the much-rejoicing fruit,
having climbed up to the glorious shoot of fair-crowned Virtue.
But come, be glorious, and in your prudent wits
neither in calamity wholly rend your heart with grief,
nor in good fortune greatly rejoice; but let your mind be gentle
toward your dear comrades and your sons and your wife,
remembering in your heart that near to men
are the gates of deadly doom and the houses of the dead;
for the race of men is like the flowers of the grass,
the flowers of spring; some wither, some grow;
therefore be gentle. And to the Argives say,
and most of all to Atreus' son Agamemnon, if in heart
they remember all I toiled about the city of Priam,
and all I plundered before I came to the Trojan soil,
let them now, in my longing, lead to my tomb,
from the spoil of Priam, fair-robed Polyxena . . .
that they may sacrifice her swiftly, since I am wroth at them
yet more even than before about Briseis; and the swell
of the sea I will stir, and cast storm upon storm,
that, wasting away by their own follies,
they may remain here a long time, until to me
they pour libations in their longing greatly for return;
but herself, if they wish, when they have taken her life,
the maiden, I do not at all grudge them to bury far off."
So speaking, he darted away, like a swift breeze;
and at once he went to the Elysian plain, where is made,
from the highest heaven, a descent and an ascent
for the immortal blessed ones; and he, when sleep left him,
remembered his father; and his noble mind was gladdened.
But when to the broad sky rose Dawn,
scattering the night, and earth and air appeared,
then the sons of the Achaeans started up from their beds
eager for return, and the ships into the depths of the sea
they were dragging, exulting in their hearts, had not
the mighty son of Achilles checked them in their haste,
and called them to assembly, and spoke his father's command:
"Hear me, dear children of the war-steadfast Argives,
the charge of my glorious father, which he told me
yesterday in my bed as I slept through the darkness;
for he said he was among the everlasting immortals;
and he bade you and the king, the son of Atreus,
that from the war you should lead a most lovely prize,
fair-robed Polyxena, to his dank tomb;
and he said that, having sacrificed her, you should bury her far off;
but if, heedless of him, you should sail the sea,
he threatened, raising adverse waves over the deep,
to keep the host together with the ships here a long time."
So he spoke; and they obeyed, and prayed to him as to a god;
for indeed in the deep the wave grew with the storm,
broader and more close-set than before,
as the wind raged; and the great sea was stirred up
by the hands of Poseidon; for to strong Achilles
he brought grace; and swiftly all the blasts rushed
upon the sea; and the Danaans, praying greatly to Achilles,
all together spoke thus to one another:
"Truly Achilles was of the race of great Zeus;
therefore now too he is a god, even if before he was among us;
for deathless time does not blot out the race of the blessed."
So speaking, they went back to the tomb of Achilles;
and they led her, as a calf to the offerings of an immortal,
which the herdsmen have torn from its mother in the thickets,
and it, lowing loud, laments, grieving in heart;
so then the daughter of Priam wailed bitterly
in the hands of the foe; and abundant tears poured from her;
as when, beneath a strong press, the fruit of the olive,
not yet blackened with the wintry rain,
pours much oil, and the gear creaks loud
beneath the cords, as the men force it;
so also from the daughter of much-enduring Priam,
dragged to the tomb of pitiless Achilles,
the dire tears, with groans, ran down her eyelids;
and her bosom beneath was filled; and her skin was wet,
truly like to costly ivory.
And then, upon her grievous griefs, a more bitter pain
fell into the heart of long-suffering Hecuba; and in her the spirit
remembered a wretched and grievous dream,
which she had seen sleeping in the night gone by;
for indeed she thought that on the tomb of godlike Achilles
she stood lamenting, and her hair to the ground
was poured from her head, and from both her breasts
ran red blood to the earth, and drenched the tomb;
fearing for this, and foreseeing great woe,
she wailed piteously, and over the lament cried aloud;
as when a bitch, lamenting before the house,
sends forth a long howling, newly torn from her milk,
whose infant young, before they could look upon the light,
the masters have cast away, to be prey for the birds,
and she, now with whining laments, now again
with howling, and a hateful cry rushes through the air;
so Hecuba, wailing, cried aloud over her daughter:
"Ah me, what first, what last, grieving in heart,
shall I wail, encompassed with many evils,
my sons or my husband, who have suffered dire and unlooked-for things,
or my city or my disgraced daughters, or my own
day of necessity and slavery? Because the terrible
Fates have entangled me in many evils.
My child, for you too, dire and unlooked-for things
the Fates have spun, even for yourself; and from your marriage they have cast
the Wedding-song, though it was near, and have brought about destruction,
unbearable and grievous and unspeakable; for indeed Achilles
even in death still warms his heart with our blood;
would that, with you, my dear child, on this day
the earth had gaped and covered me, before I saw your doom."
As she spoke, ceaselessly down her eyelids poured
the tears; for she had grief upon grief, grievously.
And when they came to the tomb of holy Achilles,
then his dear son, drawing his swift sword,
with his left hand held back the maiden, and with his right,
touching the tomb, spoke a word like this:
"Hear, father, your son who prays, and the other
Argives, and be no longer grievously wroth with us;
for now we will accomplish all that you desire
in your heart; but be gracious to us,
granting, to us who pray, swiftly a heart-cheering return."
So speaking, he drove the deadly sword through the maiden's
white throat; and at once the much-loved life left her,
as she wailed piteously at the last of her living;
and she fell forward to the ground; and beneath her neck
all was reddened, like snow, which in the mountains,
of a boar or a bear pierced through by a javelin,
swiftly grows red above with crimson blood.
And the Argives at once gave her to be borne to the city,
to the house of godlike Antenor, because he
among the Trojans, for his own noble son
Eurymachus, had reared her before as his bride.
And when he had buried the glorious daughter of Priam
near his own house, beside the sacred
tomb of Ganymede and over against the temple of the Unwearied One,
then the wave ceased, and the storm was lulled,
the terrible storm, and calm soothed the swell.
And they swiftly went to their ships, greatly exulting,
hymning the holy race of the blessed and Achilles.
And at once they took their meal, having cut the thighs of oxen
for the immortals; and lovely sacrifice was everywhere;
and they, in silver and in golden cups,
drank, drawing sweet wine; and the heart in them
rejoiced, as they longed to come to their own land.
But when they had taken their fill of supper and the feast,
then the son of Neleus spoke to them in their longing:
"Hear, friends, you who have escaped the long din of war,
that I may tell a word pleasing to your hearts in your longing;
for now is the season of heart-cheering return;
but let us go; for indeed the mighty heart of Achilles
has ceased from its grievous wrath; and the Earth-shaker
has checked the mighty wave; and gentle breezes blow;
and no longer does the wave rear up; but come, the ships
into the swell of the sea let us draw, and bethink us of return."
So he spoke to their longing; and they made ready for the voyage.
There a portent, a marvel to men on earth, appeared,
because the wife of much-bewept Priam
from a mortal became a piteous bitch; and around her the host
marvelled, gathering; and all her limbs to stone
a god turned, a great wonder even for men to come;
and her, by the promptings of Calchas, the Achaeans
set on a swift ship across the Hellespont.
And swiftly, drawing their ships into the sea,
they cast in all the goods, all that, coming to Ilium,
they had plundered before, having subdued the dwellers round about,
and all that they brought from Ilium itself, in which most
they rejoiced, since they were very many; and with them many
captive women followed, sorely grieving in heart;
and they themselves came within the ships. But to them Calchas
did not follow as they hastened into the sea, but the other
Argives too he kept back; for about the Capherean rocks
he feared a dire destruction rushing upon the Danaans.
But they obeyed him not at all; for an evil fate
beguiled the minds of men; and alone, well knowing the prophecies,
Amphilochus, the swift son of blameless Amphiaraus,
remained together with wise Calchas; for to them it was
fated, both of them, far from their own land,
to the cities of the Pamphylians and Cilicians to come.
But these things the gods set for afterward; and the Achaeans
loosed their ships' cables from the land, and their anchors
swiftly raised; and the Hellespont rang
as they hastened; and the ships were washed about by the sea;
and around them, about the prows, lay many
arms of the slain; and above, tokens of victory,
countless, were hung aloft; and they crowned the ships
both with garlands and with spears and with shields, with which they fought
against the foe; and from the prows the lords
poured into the dark sea much wine to the gods,
praying to the blessed ones to grant a return free from grief;
and their prayers were mingled with the winds, and far from the ships
in vain were borne off together with the clouds and the air.
And the captive women gazed back toward Ilium, grieving in heart,
and much, lamenting, they wailed,
hiding from the Argives the great grief in their hearts;
and some held their hands about their knees; and others their foreheads
propped upon their hands, the wretched ones; and others their children
held in their arms; and these did not yet groan for the day of slavery
nor for their fatherland's woes, but at the breast
held their hearts; for far from sorrows is an infant's heart.
And the hair of all was loosed, and their grievous breasts
were torn about with their nails; and on their cheeks the tears
lay dry, and others above flowed down
thick from their eyelids; and they beheld their wretched fatherland
still wholly ablaze, and the much smoke rising;
and about glorious Cassandra, gazing,
they all looked, remembering her grievous prophecy;
and she laughed at them as they wailed,
though grieving herself at the hateful woes of her fatherland.
And of the Trojans, all who escaped from the pitiless war,
gathering through the city, laboured about the corpses,
eager to bury them; and to the grievous work Antenor
led them; and on a single pyre they laid many.
And the Argives, exulting ceaselessly in their hearts,
now with their oars clove the dark water,
now with eager haste made ready the sails on their ships;
and behind them swiftly was left all
Dardania and the tomb of Achilles; and they in their hearts,
though rejoicing, remembering the slain, with one mind
grievously grieved, and toward a foreign land
they cast their eyes. And it appeared to them far from the ships,
receding; and they swiftly were borne past the surf
of sea-girt Tenedos; and they passed Chryse
and the holy seat of Sminthian Phoebus and divine Cilla;
and windy Lesbos appeared; and they rounded the cape
swiftly of Lectum, where is the last headland of Ida.
And the swelling sails roared round; and about the prows
the dark swell crashed; and the long waves
were darkened; and the sea-paths whitened over the deep.
And now the Argives would have come to the holy soil of Hellas,
all of them, over the deep of the sea unharmed, had not
the daughter of loud-thundering Zeus, Athena, been wroth with them;
and when they came near windy Euboea,
then, devising a heavy and pitiless doom
for the king of the Locrians, and chafing unbearably,
she stood beside Zeus, lord of the gods, and spoke a word
apart from the immortals; and her heart could not contain its wrath:
"Father Zeus, no longer are the deeds men devise endurable
to the gods, men who heed in their minds neither yourself
nor the other blessed ones, since now vengeance no longer follows
wretched men, but often the noble man
is borne down more by woes, and has unceasing misery;
therefore no one any longer reveres justice, nor is there shame
among men; I for my part will neither in Olympus
be, nor be called yours any longer, unless of the Achaeans
I take vengeance for their recklessness, since indeed within my temple
the son of Oileus greatly transgressed against me, nor did he pity
Cassandra, stretching her heedless hands toward me
many times, nor did he fear my might, nor in his heart
did he reverence the immortal, but wrought an unbearable deed.
Therefore now, in your immortal heart, do not grudge me
to do as my spirit desires, that others too,
the warriors, may tremble at the gods' clear threat."
To her as she spoke the father answered with gentle words:
"My child, I in no way oppose you for the sake of the Achaeans,
but all the gear, which before, bringing grace to me,
with their unwearied hands the Cyclopes fashioned,
I will give you in your longing; but you, with your strong heart,
yourself stir a grievous storm upon the Argives."
So speaking, the swift lightning and the deadly thunderbolt
and the groaning thunder, near the fearless maiden
he set; and her heart was greatly gladdened within.
And at once she put on the rushing aegis, all-gleaming,
unbreakable and strong and a wonder to the immortals;
for upon it was wrought the head of grim Medusa,
terrible; and strong serpents, breathing the rush
of unwearied fire, fierce, were above it;
and the whole aegis rang about the breast of the queen,
as when the boundless sky roars with the lightnings.
And she took her father's arms, which no god lifts
save great Zeus; and she shook tall Olympus;
and she poured together the clouds and all the air above;
and night was poured about the earth, and the sea grew dark;
and Zeus looked on and greatly rejoiced; and the broad
sky moved about the feet of the goddess; and the air rang round,
as when unwearied Zeus rushes eagerly to the fray.
And straightway, to be borne over the misty sea,
she sent from heaven to Aeolus immortal Iris,
that he might send all the winds together, bearing down,
to come near the rugged heights of Caphereus,
ceaselessly driven, and to swell up the sea,
maddened with grievous blasts. And she, hearing,
swiftly darted, wrapped about with clouds;
you would have said there was fire together with the air and the black water.
And she came to Aeolia, where, of the winds that blow fierce,
the caves are, fitted about with hard rocks,
hollow and echoing; and close by are the halls
of Aeolus, son of Hippotas. And she found him within
with his wife and twelve children; and she told him
all that Athena was devising against the return of the Danaans.
And he did not disobey, but, going outside the halls,
with his unwearied hands he struck a great mountain with his trident,
where the winds, loud-sounding and ill-sounding, were housed
in a hollow cavern; and ever a cry rang round,
bellowing grievously; and by force he broke the height.
And they at once poured out; and he bade them all,
gathering a dark tempest together, to blow, that the grievous
swell of the rising sea might cover the heights of Caphereus.
And they swiftly arose before they heard from their king
all his word; and as they rushed, the sea groaned
unbearably; and like to steep mountains the waves
were borne, one here, one there. And the heart of the Achaeans
was broken in their breasts, since the wave now
bore the ship high through the air, and now again
bore them, as if rolling down a cliff,
into the misty depths; and a force unbearable ever
spurted up the sand as the surge parted.
And they, smitten with helplessness, neither upon the oar
could lay a hand in their dismay, nor the sails,
strong though they longed, could haul up about the yards,
as they broke from the winds, nor steer back again
to the voyage; for grievous storms drove on around them;
nor had the helmsmen any longer strength of the ships
with their skilled hands swiftly to ply the steering-oars;
for all things this way and that the evil blasts confounded.
Nor was there any hope of life, because dark
night together with the great storm and the dire wrath of the immortals
arose; for Poseidon stirred up the pitiless sea,
bringing grace to his brother's glorious daughter,
who herself too, from above, raging pitilessly,
rushed amid the lightnings; and Zeus thundered from heaven,
glorifying his child in his heart; and all around
the islands and the mainlands were flooded by the sea,
not far from Euboea, where most
the deity wrought, upon pitiless griefs, fresh griefs,
for the Argives. And groaning and wailing throughout the ships
arose of the perishing; and the timbers of the ships crashed
as they broke; for they, crowded close upon one another,
ever shattered together; and toil unending arose.
And some, eager with their oars to thrust off
the ships that rushed upon them, with the very timbers, wretched,
fell into the great deep, and beneath pitiless doom
died, because upon them from this side and that bore down
the long timbers of the ships; and the bodies of all
were crushed together grievously; and others, fallen in the ships,
lay like to the dead; and others, by necessity,
swam, clinging to the well-polished oars;
and others again floated upon the planks; and the brine roared
from the depth, so that the sea and the sky and the land too
appeared all joined together to one another.
And she of Olympus, the loud-thundering Unwearied One,
in no way shamed her father's might; and around her the air
rang. And she, bringing wrath and woe to Ajax,
cast a thunderbolt upon his ship; and at once, this way and that,
she scattered it in little pieces; and earth and air rang round;
and all of encircling Amphitrite was swept over.
And they fell out of the ship in a throng; and around them
the long waves were borne; and in the lightnings of the queen
a gleam flashed, darting through the darkness;
and they, gulping the undrinkable brine of the much-sounding sea,
breathing out their lives, were borne over the deep.
And to the captive women, even as they perished, came joy;
and some of them sank into the sea, casting
their arms about their children, the wretched ones; and others grievously
cast their hands about the heads of the foe, with whom, baleful,
they hastened to perish, taking vengeance on the Danaans,
worthy of their own outrage; and she, looking down from above,
rejoiced in her heart, noble Tritogeneia.
And Ajax now swam about a timber of the ship,
now again with his hands traversed the briny depths,
like to the unwearied Titan in his overweening might;
and the briny swell was cloven about the strong hands
of the high-hearted man; and the gods, beholding him,
marvelled at his manhood and strength; and about him the wave
now bore him huge, as upon the peak
of a high mountain through the air, now again
from on high, as in ravines, hid him; but he his hands
wearied not, much-enduring; and many on this side and that,
quenched, the thunderbolts crackled into the sea;
for not yet did the daughter of loud-thundering Zeus
devise to subdue his spirit with doom, much though she was wroth,
before he had endured many evils and toiled utterly in griefs;
therefore in the deep misery long laid him low,
tormented on every side; for round about boundless evils the Fates
set about the man; but necessity breathed strength into him;
and he said that, even if all the Olympians came together into one,
in wrath, and raised the whole sea,
he would escape; but in no way did he escape the gods' threat;
for the overweening Earth-shaker was wroth with him,
when he saw him clinging with his hand to the rock
of Gyrae, and he was greatly enraged at him; and he shook
the sea together with the boundless land; and everywhere round
the cliffs of Caphereus were thrown into turmoil; and the grievous
surf, beaten, crashed with the fierce swell
of the wrathful lord; and he broke off into the sea a broad
rock, which that man was grasping with his hands.
And as he writhed about the crags for a very long while,
his hands were stripped, and blood ran beneath his nails;
and the murmuring wave ever, as it was stirred about him,
whitened with foam his head and shaggy chin;
and now he would have escaped his evil doom, had not against him . . .
breaking the earth beneath, he hurled up a peak;
as before, against great Enceladus, wise
Pallas, lifting up the Sicilian island, cast it down,
which still ever burns beneath the unwearied Giant
breathing smoking fire within the earth; so the king
of the Locrians the height of the mountain covered, the wretched man,
falling down from above, and weighed down the strong man;
and about him black destruction of death came upon him,
subdued together by land and by the barren sea.
And so also the other Achaeans were borne over the great gulf,
some on their ships in dismay, others fallen
outside the ships; and deadly misery held them all;
for some of the ships were borne sidelong in the sea,
others, turned over, with keel uppermost; and of some the masts
were broken off from the beams as the wind drove on;
and of others the swift storms scattered all the timbers;
and others into the great deep sank beneath,
as the boundless rain bore down, nor did they withstand
the fierce water of the sea together with the rain of Zeus,
mingled; for like a river the air flowed
unceasing; and below the divine sea raged.
And one said: "Surely such a storm came upon men once,
when the unspeakable rain of Deucalion came,
and the earth became sea, and the deep poured over all."
So spoke one of the Danaans, dismayed in heart at the storm,
grievous; and many perished; and about the dead
the great swell of the sea was filled, and all the shores
were thronged; for the wave spat out many onto the dry land;
and about the ships' timbers all of heavy-roaring Amphitrite
it covered utterly; and the wave appeared in the midst.
And one drew this evil doom, another that; some over the broad
sea, as the brine was stirred, unbearable, and others on the rocks,
having shattered their ships, perished wretchedly
by the contriving of Nauplius; for he, greatly wroth for his son,
as the storm arose and the Argives perished,
though grieving, greatly rejoiced, because to him
the god granted vengeance swiftly, and he saw the hated throng
tormented in the deep, and to his own father much
he prayed that all might perish together with the ships, sunk beneath.
And Poseidon heard him well, and brought them all near
the dark swell; and he, like a mountain-mule, with his hand a pine,
blazing, raised aloft; and by guile he brought the Achaeans near,
hoping to reach the well-harboured seat of havens;
for terribly about the hard rocks they were subdued,
with their very ships; and upon their evil a more bitter pain
they endured, dashed against the grievous rocks
in the swift night; and few escaped doom, whom there saved
either a god or some helping deity; but Athena
now in her heart greatly rejoiced, now again
grieved for wise Odysseus, because he was to suffer
many pains by the threat of Poseidon,
who then, in his unwearied heart utterly grudging
the walls and towers of the mighty Argives,
which they had toiled to make a defence against the hateful war-cry of the Trojans,
swiftly flooded the whole sea over them,
all that comes down from the Euxine to the Hellespont,
and cast it on the shores of Troy; and from above rained
Zeus, bringing grace to the glorious Earth-shaker;
nor indeed was the Far-worker free from toil,
but from the Idaean mountains all the streams
he gathered into one place, and flooded the work of the Achaeans;
and the sea was swept over, and still the roaring
torrents went, grievously swollen with the rain of Zeus,
which the dark swell of much-groaning Amphitrite kept back
from coming over the sea, before they had laid in ashes
all the walls of the Danaans grievously; and Poseidon himself
broke the earth beneath, and there gushed up boundless water
and mud and sand; and with his strong might he shook
Sigeum; and the shores roared loud, and the foundations
of Dardania, and, made unseen and sunk beneath,
the boundless rampart was hidden, and it sank within the earth
as it parted wide; and the sand alone still appeared
as the sea drew back, and from the loud-roaring shores
it was stretched out, far from the beach. But these things, I think,
the evil purpose of the immortals accomplished; and they in their ships,
the Argives, sailed, all whom the storm had scattered;
and one came one way, another another, where the god led each,
all who over the sea escaped the baleful blasts.
